pages.title: About the firm
pages.content:
About the firm

Hoshi Wealth Partners opened in Seattle in 2009, named for founding partner Naomi Hoshi-Clarke.

The firm is fee-only and has stayed small on purpose: seven people, one table, and about one hundred forty households.

pages.title: People
pages.content:
People

Seven people share one table at 1418 Western Avenue, Suite 600.

Naomi Hoshi-Clarke, Tomás Ferreira, Priya Raman, Henrik Aalto, Grace Mwangi, Samuel Ortiz-Bell and Lena Fischer.

pages.title: Approach
pages.content:
Approach

Fewer moves, better reasons.

Every household starts with a written investment policy, low-cost index funds and a rebalance by written rule.

pages.title: Services
pages.content:
Services

Planning, retirement income, investment management, and tax and estate coordination.

All of it sits in one written plan, and custody stays at an independent custodian.

pages.title: Fees
pages.content:
Fees

The invoice is the only payment: no commissions, no product fees, no performance fees.

The first meeting is $0; a written financial plan is $4,800; the ongoing planning retainer is $7,200 a year.

Each story is a composite. Nothing here is a result.

posts.title: A written investment policy, before the portfolio.
posts.excerpt: Before any fund is chosen, each household gets a written investment policy: what the money is for, how long it can stay invested, and what would make the firm change course.
posts.content:
Before any fund is chosen, each household at Hoshi Wealth Partners gets a written investment policy. It is a short document, usually two pages, and it answers three questions: what is this money for, how long can it stay invested, and what would make us change course.

The policy is written at the table, with the adviser and the household together. It names the asset mix and the rule for rebalancing, and it names who decides what. Because it is written first, the portfolio that follows has a reason for every holding.

Once a year the policy is read again. It is rewritten only when the household's life has changed, not because a quarter felt urgent. Nothing in it is a forecast, and nothing in it is a promise about the next twelve months.

posts.title: What a quarterly report is for.
posts.excerpt: A quarterly report says what the firm did, what it cost, and what is unchanged. It carries no forecast.
posts.content:
A quarterly report has three jobs. It says what the firm did in the last three months, what that cost, and what is unchanged. That is all.

Most quarters the honest answer to the first question is very little: a rebalance because a rule said so, perhaps a withdrawal for the household's monthly income. The cost is shown in dollars, not only as a percentage, so a household can see exactly what the invoice bought.

The report has no forecast and no market commentary written to sound clever. If the written investment policy is working, the report should be short and a little dull. That is the point.

posts.title: Why the firm stays small.
posts.excerpt: Seven people, one table and about one hundred forty households: why Hoshi Wealth Partners has kept the firm small on purpose.
posts.content:
Hoshi Wealth Partners has seven people and about one hundred forty households. That ratio is a decision, not an accident. Naomi Hoshi-Clarke opened the firm in 2009 so that a family could sit with the same adviser year after year.

A small firm can keep its promises to individual households. The person who wrote your plan still answers the phone, and the partners read every quarterly report before it is sent. When a household's life changes, the people who need to know are in the same room.

If the firm ever grows, it will be by adding a table, not by stretching one. For now, seven people share one reading room on Western Avenue, and that is enough.
